issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Situations: Sexual situations or intimacy

The rest of the profile centers on generic hyperarousal/dissociation and transportation-related cues, so these two triggers do not fit the trauma-specific pattern and weaken Triggers → Threat / Triggers → Memory coherence.

For this trauma type, permanent humiliation is insufficiently supported by the other selected items.

Undereating does not plausibly address any represented symptom cluster and feels disconnected from the threat/memory/appraisal pattern.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Open Spaces: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
issues.explanation: 'Avoid open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on transportation cues, startle/physical threat reactions, and trauma memory phenomena from an MVC. Open-space avoidance suggests a different threat pattern (e.g., assault/agoraphobic vulnerability) that is not represented elsewhere.

A bicycle-specific trigger is difficult to reconcile with a life-threatening motor vehicle collision unless the collision specifically involved a bicycle; the rest of the profile is vehicle/crash focused rather than bicycle focused, so this item stands out as trauma-incongruent.

issues.item: Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
issues.explanation: Alarm to unexpected touch suggests an interpersonal/assault-related threat cue more than a motor vehicle collision. In the context of the other threat items, generic startle and physical reactivity fit, but touch-specific alarm is not well linked to the reported trauma or the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere
issues.explanation: 'I no longer belong anywhere' is a broad social-identity appraisal that is not impossible, but it sits awkwardly with the otherwise self-blame/competence-focused appraisal pattern tied to an MVC. It is less clearly connected to the memory and trigger content than more trauma-specific appraisals would be.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
issues.explanation: Restricting food as a coping strategy is not impossible, but here it is poorly supported by the rest of the profile. The formulation strongly links threat and appraisals to maladaptive strategies, and the other strategies are vehicle avoidance and thought monitoring, whereas undereating addresses a symptom domain not otherwise represented.

vignette:
Walter is a sixty-seven-year-old widower who worked for decades as a military medic, a job that had trained him to stay calm under fire and to trust his hands no matter what. He lives alone in a small house on a quiet street, and for the past two years he has not driven a car and has avoided being a passenger in one as well. That began after the accident: a clear autumn afternoon, a four-lane highway, a pickup truck that crossed the median and hit his sedan head-on. Walter remembers the moment of impact but not the seconds before or after; what stays with him is the smell of burnt rubber and gasoline that filled the cabin, and the sound of metal tearing, a sound he can still hear in his head when the memory surfaces, as if it is playing through a speaker in a room he cannot leave. The other driver was later found to have a blood-alcohol level three times the legal limit. Walter spent two weeks in the hospital with a fractured pelvis and a concussion.

In the months that followed, Walter found he could no longer sit in a car without his heart slamming against his ribs and his hands going slick with sweat. At first he thought it was just nerves, that he would get over it, but the physical reaction grew worse rather than better. He stopped accepting rides from his neighbor, stopped going to the grocery store except on foot, stopped visiting his son and daughter-in-law because they lived a twenty-minute drive away. Being a passenger made him feel trapped, helpless, certain that another collision was only a moment away. He did not consciously decide to isolate himself; the choice felt like the only safe one. It was not just cars, though. One evening a few months after the accident, his neighbor invited him over for a beer. Walter walked into the backyard and the smell hit him-the sharp, yeasty scent of an open bottle, rising from a plastic cup on the picnic table. His throat closed. His vision tunneled. For a second he was back in the sedan, the smell of the other driver's breath mingling with the burnt rubber, a sour odor he had not even registered until that moment but that now flooded his senses. He made an excuse and left, and after that he stopped going anywhere near the liquor store on his street, avoided the bar his son sometimes suggested, and hurried past anyone who was drinking on a porch. The smell of alcohol-even a faint trace on a passerby's breath-could land him right back in the crumpled car, heart hammering, mouth dry.

What frightened him most, though, was something interior. In the quiet of his house, Walter began to watch his own thoughts. He would catch himself thinking about the crash and then panic, wondering if dwelling on it meant he was losing his mind. He started to try hard not to think about the event at all, but the effort itself became a kind of vigilance. He would notice a smell-once, the neighbor was grilling and the charred meat sent him straight back to the burnt odor in the wrecked car-and his body would react before his mind caught up: his stomach dropped, his jaw clenched, and he felt a surge of adrenaline that made no sense for a barbecue. Another time, a delivery driver stepped out of a van with a faint whiff of beer on his clothes, and Walter had to brace himself against the doorframe to keep from shaking. He became jumpy at ordinary sounds: a truck backfiring down the street, a pan dropping in the kitchen, a door closing too sharply. Each time he startled, he told himself he was a coward, a weak person who could not handle what plenty of other people handled every day.

The memory itself felt strange to him. When he tried to describe the accident to his doctor, his words got tangled and he lost the thread halfway through, as though the story belonged to someone else and he was only a poor narrator. Sometimes he would sit and wonder if he had actually done something wrong, if he had acted too slowly or failed to see the truck in time, even though the police report had been clear: the other driver was drunk, there was nothing Walter could have done. But that knowledge did not shake the conviction that the event happened because of the way he behaved-that he had missed some signal, some duty of alertness that a good medic never misses. He came to believe he could not trust his own judgment anymore. If he had failed that day, how could he trust himself to do the right thing in anything else? The smell of alcohol especially seemed to mock that doubt: every time he caught a whiff, he felt a sick certainty that he had missed something about the other driver's state, had failed to anticipate what anyone with good instincts would have seen coming.

The weeks turned into a year, then two. His son called every Sunday and could hear the flatness in Walter's voice, but Walter always said he was fine, just tired. He avoided talking about the accident because talking about it meant thinking about it, and thinking about it made him feel as though he was falling apart. He began to notice that his own mind felt like an enemy he had to police: he would check what he was thinking every few minutes, looking for signs of craziness-a memory popping up, a vivid sound, a flash of the crumpled hood, a phantom whiff of beer or gasoline. He told himself this was the only way to stay in control. What finally brought Walter to seek help was not his own distress but something his son said over the phone last week. "Dad, you haven't left the house in two months. You don't even try. That's not you." Walter hung up and sat in the dark living room, and for the first time he acknowledged that maybe he could not fix this alone. He called a clinic the next morning. He still does not know exactly what he hopes for-maybe just to stop being afraid of his own thoughts, maybe to believe that he is not as weak as he feels, maybe to walk past a liquor store without his stomach dropping. But he also fears that if he really opens the door to the memory, he will find out that he really is going crazy, that he will never drive again, that the crash will have taken everything it touched.
